JAH-REL-010031.title: The Choir of Small Hours — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010031.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the night singers' faith. The Choir of Small Hours is a fictional faith of the night singers: they hold that the hours between midnight and dawn are sacred, and the keeping of them is the worship. Their central metaphor is the vigil — the world sleeps, and the choir keeps watch. Their practices are the night hymn (sung softly, at 3 a.m.), the lamp tending (one lamp per household, never dark), and the dawn greeting (the first light, welcomed aloud). Their teaching: the dark is not the absence of light but its cradle. Their ethic: never let a neighbor's lamp go out. Their tension: the choir loves the night, but the dawn always comes — and they greet it anyway.

JAH-REL-010032.title: The Order of the Patient Seed — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010032.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the gardeners' faith. The Order of the Patient Seed is a fictional faith of the gardeners: they hold that the seed knows the season, and the gardener's work is the waiting. Their central metaphor is the germination — the invisible work before the green. Their practices are the seed blessing (each planting, spoken), the weeding meditation (the slow hour, weekly), and the harvest sharing (the first fruits, given away). Their teaching: growth cannot be hurried, only tended. Their ethic: plant for the seventh generation. Their tension: the gardener wants the harvest now, but the seed keeps its own time — and the order learns to wait.

JAH-REL-010033.title: The Lanterns of the Long Night — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010033.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the winter light faith. The Lanterns of the Long Night is a fictional faith of the winter keepers: they hold that the longest night is the year's holiest, and the lanterns are the prayers. Their central metaphor is the carried light — each lantern a hope, walked through the dark. Their practices are the lantern walk (the solstice procession), the window lighting (a candle for every traveler), and the story night (the tales told till dawn). Their teaching: the light is brightest when it's carried. Their ethic: no traveler walks the long night alone. Their tension: the winter always returns, but so do the lanterns — and the walk goes on.

JAH-REL-010034.title: The Covenant of Open Doors — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010034.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the hospitality faith. The Covenant of Open Doors is a fictional faith of hospitality: they hold that the stranger is the sacred guest, and the open door is the altar. Their central metaphor is the threshold — the line between outside and welcome. Their practices are the guest bread (baked for whoever comes), the empty chair (always set, always ready), and the farewell blessing (the road made kind). Their teaching: the host is blessed by the guest, not the reverse. Their ethic: turn no one away. Their tension: the open door invites the difficult guest too — and the covenant holds anyway.

JAH-REL-010035.title: The Way of the Mended Net — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010035.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the fishers' faith. The Way of the Mended Net is a fictional faith of the fishers: they hold that the torn net mended is holier than the net never torn. Their central metaphor is the mending — the patient knots, the restored whole. Their practices are the net-mending circle (the torn things, brought together), the catch sharing (the haul divided by need), and the storm prayer (the sea respected, never commanded). Their teaching: breakage is the beginning of the stronger. Their ethic: mend what the storm tore, in nets and in neighbors. Their tension: the sea gives and takes — and the way mends on.

JAH-REL-010036.title: The Keepers of the Common Well — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010036.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the water faith. The Keepers of the Common Well is a fictional faith of the water keepers: they hold that the well belongs to all, and the keeping is the worship. Their central metaphor is the drawn water — the daily gift, the shared source. Their practices are the morning drawing (the first bucket, in silence), the well cleaning (the communal work, monthly), and the drought sharing (the rationing, by need). Their teaching: water is the commons made visible. Their ethic: the well never runs dry for the keeper's neighbor. Their tension: the dry years test the keeping — and the keepers share anyway.

JAH-REL-010037.title: The Feast of First Light — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010037.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the dawn feast faith. The Feast of First Light is a fictional faith of the dawn keepers: they hold that the first light of significant days is sacred, and the feast honors it. Their central metaphor is the breaking — the night broken by the light, the fast broken by the feast. Their practices are the dawn watch (the waiting, together), the first-light meal (eaten facing east), and the light sharing (the day's first kindness, done before noon). Their teaching: every dawn is the first. Their ethic: greet the light by being light. Their tension: the cloudy dawns hide the sun — and the feast goes on anyway.

JAH-REL-010038.title: The Circle of the Unfinished Song — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010038.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the singers' faith. The Circle of the Unfinished Song is a fictional faith of the singers: they hold that the song is never finished, only continued, and the singing is the worship. Their central metaphor is the verse — each generation adds its own. Their practices are the circle singing (the rounds, unending), the verse adding (the new words, welcomed), and the listening (the silence between, honored). Their teaching: the song outlives the singer. Their ethic: teach the song to the young. Their tension: the verses disagree across generations — and the circle sings them all.

JAH-REL-010039.title: The Pilgrims of the Quiet Road — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010039.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the walkers' faith. The Pilgrims of the Quiet Road is a fictional faith of the walkers: they hold that the road walked slowly is the prayer, and the destination is the excuse. Their central metaphor is the step — the single step, repeated in faith. Their practices are the slow walking (the pilgrimage pace), the road kindness (the help given to fellow walkers), and the arrival gratitude (the thanks at the journey's end). Their teaching: the road teaches what the temple cannot. Their ethic: walk gently; leave the road better. Their tension: the road is long and the feet tire — and the pilgrims walk on.

JAH-REL-010040.title: The Archive of Borrowed Stories — Fictional Tradition (Edition 1)
JAH-REL-010040.description: FICTIONAL worldbuilding tradition (not a real religion): the storytellers' faith. The Archive of Borrowed Stories is a fictional faith of the storytellers: they hold that every story is borrowed, and the borrowing is the sacred trust. Their central metaphor is the lending — the tale told, returned, retold. Their practices are the story keeping (the tales recorded faithfully), the story lending (the telling, freely given), and the story returning (the credit to the source, always). Their teaching: the storyteller owns nothing and carries everything. Their ethic: never steal a story; always borrow it well. Their tension: the best stories want to be kept — and the archive lends them anyway.
